html:
The Secret History of the Mongols is the oldest surviving work of Mongolian literature. It was written for the Mongol royal family some time after the death of Genghis Khan in 1227, and tells his life and conquests and part of the reign of his son Ögedei.

The author is unknown. The book ends by saying it was finished in a Year of the Mouse at an assembly on the Kherlen River. That could be 1228, 1240 or 1252; many scholars favour 1240.

It is not a dry chronicle. It mixes prose and verse and is full of vivid scenes:

  • the legend of the Mongols' ancestor, a blue-grey wolf
  • Temüjin's hungry childhood after his father's death
  • his friendship and then war with Jamukha
  • quarrels among his sons about who should succeed him

It is the only full account of Genghis Khan from the Mongol side. Persian and Chinese histories, such as Rashid al-Din's Compendium of Chronicles, drew on related material.

The original, written in the Uyghur-Mongolian script, is lost. The text survived because early in the Ming dynasty, after the fall of the Yuan, Chinese officials wrote down its sounds in Chinese characters, with a Chinese gloss, to train interpreters. Scholars rebuilt the Mongolian text from that version.

Today it is a national classic in Mongolia and the main source on the steppe world in which the Mongol Empire was born.
